title: Blackout City is out on mobile — using AI for code and story art, then checking whether the scene actually makes sense
author: Sobitech
selftext:
I’m the developer of **Blackout City**, a turn-based robot-swapping puzzle made in Godot, now released on Android and iOS. AI tools were used for coding assistance and image generation, as well as revising and localizing the story. I wanted to share a specific review problem from that process alongside the game.

# A good-looking panel can still tell the wrong story

One scene showed a resident helping an older man, but its dialogue addressed a named character who wasn’t the person depicted. There were also mismatches between the speaker label, the people visible, and the way those characters would speak to each other.

That led to a pass checking each scene as a conversation: who is pictured, who is speaking, who is listening, and what those two people would actually say in that situation. This mattered particularly in Korean, where the level of politeness helps establish the relationship. A natural sentence could still feel wrong when assigned to the wrong speaker.

# Reviewing the story in the form players encounter it

We revised the prose to read more like fiction and worked on making the in-game dialogue carry the story even for someone who knew nothing about the city. We also moved the story beyond the small section of the result screen, giving it dedicated scenes and a place to revisit what had been unlocked. Matching text to the illustrations became part of that review, rather than treating the two as finished independently.

The game supports 12 languages. For me, a useful question during this process was whether someone could follow the scene from the picture and dialogue together. That exposed problems which a line-by-line wording review didn’t catch.

# The puzzle underneath

Dragging one robot swaps it with each teammate along the route. Getting it to the destination is only half the problem: you also have to consider where its teammates end up. Moving the robot that carries power can break a connection; shifting a shield can expose a facility to an attack. Later puzzles combine power routing, defense, stored energy, and transporting teammates.

There’s no timer while you think, but each stage has a turn limit. Undo is free, and cleared stages can be revisited for fewer turns and three stars.

If you’ve used generated illustrations in a story-driven game, how do you keep character identity, dialogue voice, and the visible action consistent across scenes and translations? I’d be interested in what you check before calling a panel finished.
